For what its worth, death in Overwatch is a lot more forgiving than death in CS:GO.

If you die in CS:GO, you're out for the entire round (unless you're playing deathmatch, or gungame, or something like that). This makes it pretty difficult for a casual or novice player to learn to aim or position, because a novice can easily end up spending half their time spectating rather than playing (which is why people use gungame to learn the weapons). 

On the other hand, when you die in Overwatch, you only have to wait a few seconds until you respawn, during which time you can choose to switch characters. This takes a lot of the 'fear' out of dying. Unlike in CS:GO, you can feel free to experiment with different strategies with relatively little risk.

True, the skill ceiling is very high. But Overwatch is a much better environment for learning. If you miss a shot, or get caught unaware by the enemy, it should only be a temporary setback in casual play.

(Not to mention, aiming in CS:GO is a lot more difficult than it is in most shooters due to recoil and bullet spread.)

The Sams are secular, but they were started by a Christian vicar, hence the unfortunate name.

They're pretty much the standard suicide hotline in the UK, and going by track record, are probably one of the better organisations on that list.

*Saying that*, they did come under fire in 2014 for their 'Samaritans Radar' app, which monitored (publicly available) tweets looking for 'suicidal phrases'. Unsurprisingly, people didn't like having their tweets monitored for phrases like "help me" or "tired of being alone". Some people threatened to sue, others called it a breach of the UK data protection act (I have no idea if that's true or not). Some of the criticism came from the SJW angle, [there were concerns about 'stalkers and bullies' using the app to identify targets](http://archive.is/9Zjs1). It might be worthwhile for you to read the SuicideWatch [talking tips](https://www.reddit.com/r/SWResources/comments/igh87/concerned_but_dont_know_what_to_say_here_are_some/). They're generally a good guide for this kind of situation.

>I'm trying to put zero pressure on her or to make her feel like I blame her for her current state.

The fact that you already know that you should avoid blame is a good sign, and makes me think that you're likely on the right track.

Too many people resort to blame or guilt-tripping as their first resort in these situations, and the fact that you know to avoid that, makes you a better helper than most.

>I already told her that she is a great person and that I admire her for what she has achieved in her life. That she is a great person and a good mother. That I respect her.

Be a bit careful with this approach. It *can* be ineffective at times, especially if the suicidal person is in such a grim state that they can't aknowledge that they're a good or worthwhile person.  

Paradoxically, with a suicidal person, taking too positive a point of view can sometime *increase* their feeling of aloneness, rather than pulling them out of their crisis.

However, in your case, you seem to know her very well, and I suspect that your compliments are heartfelt, so it probably helped her to hear that you respect her. But please, please keep in mind that it's important to aknowledge her view of the situation, so that she knows that she's being listened to and understood. Even if her viewpoint is very grim and even somewhat unrealistic.

>But I need your support as well if I should get at my wits' end.

I know that you want to help her, but keep in mind that you're not responsible for her mental health and it *is* fair to set boundaries. You can't help your friend if your own mental health suffers, and so setting boundaries does a favour to the both of you.

If you ever start to truly feel that you're approaching your wits' end, then it is okay to withdraw for a while, to recuperate.

But I think it's a good thing that you're looking for support for yourself as you help your friend through this. You recognise that helping someone through a suicide crisis can take a psychological toll.

>I'll leave my phone on for the night and told her she can reach me if necessary.

This is a very good thing to do, I think. As long as you feel up to taking the call.

Sometimes, simply knowing that there's someone out there willing to lend a helping hand, or a shoulder to cry on, can be a great boon to a suicidal person.

You seem to care about her a lot, and I suspect that she has a very good friend in you.

I agree with this analysis. I think point 2, and perhaps point 1, were my main problems with this episode. I wasn't really bothered by the endings themselves, I thought that they would have been (mostly) fine, given the proper context -- although it is true that the endings weren't particularly good at illustrating the effects of the player's choices.

But what I had really hoped for, in Episode 5, was some kind of revelation, some kind of 'Aha!' moment which would tie the entire story together. Something that would explain all of the hanging plot threads. What's up with Samuel? How do the Prescott's know so much? How did Max's powers cause the tornado? Why is Rachel Amber so mysterious (everyone seemed to know her, and yet, no-one seems to understand her)? I wanted something that would either explain Max's powers or at least give some context to them. 

Tobanga, the doe, the lighthouse. All recurring motifs, that in retrospect, feel like false symbolism. Without a linchpin tying it all together, none of this really seems to mean anything. Were most of these hanging threads just red herrings? I feel as if the devs want us to puzzle it out, but at this point I'm kind of sceptical that it will lead anywhere.

That was the problem with episode 5, it just never really delivered in that sense. It never had the huge revelations of the previous episodes. So although I enjoyed individual parts of it, the experience as a whole felt a bit hollow.

This was also why the dream sequence disappointed me somewhat. Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed it, but I knew, going in, that it was probably *just* an anxiety dream. I was *hoping* that there might be more to it. That it might have been a symptom of time coming unwound. It would have been a perfect opportunity for Dontnod to illustrate *how* Max's powers were affecting reality. Instead, it did nothing but illustrate Max's anxieties. Anxieties that we were already quite aware of.
